subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Napoleon's Continental Blockade and Chicory Coffee
description: A fast breakdown of Napoleon's Continental Blockade and Chicory Coffee for builders.

hook.text: When Napoleon blockaded European ports in 1806, coffee imports stopped. France and Germany desperately sought substitutes.

buildup.text: Real coffee became impossibly expensive. People tried roasted barley, acorns, and figs as replacements—all terrible.

discovery.text: Chicory root—roasted and ground—became the most successful substitute. It was bitter, dark, and vaguely coffee-like.

twist.text: New Orleans still blends chicory with coffee today. The tradition came from French colonists who survived Napoleon's blockade.

climax.text: The blockade proved coffee's hold on Europe. People chose fake substitutes over abandoning the ritual.

punchline.text: No ships, no beans, roasted roots instead. War couldn't kill the coffee habit.

quiz.question: Why does New Orleans still use chicory in its coffee?
options: The tradition came from French colonists who used it during Napoleon's blockade
